chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
"His sacrifice (hady) suffices for him in the Udhiyah (Qurbani)." And the reason for the hair-marking (ish'ar) of the camel and the tagging (taqlid) is what has been narrated:

key_terms.إِشْعَارُ: Marking or shaving a part of the hair (of the sacrificial animal)
key_terms.التَّقْلِيدُ: Tagging or putting a ring in the nose of the animal for identification
key_terms.الْأُضْحِيَّةُ: The sacrificial animal offered during Eid al-Adha
key_terms.الْبَدَنَةُ: A young camel (five years old) used for sacrifice
key_terms.الْعِلَّةُ: The legal reason or cause behind a ruling
key_terms.هَدْيُهُ: His sacrifice/hady, referring to the animal offered for ritual purposes

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling regarding the sufficiency of the sacrificial animal for Udhiyah and the reasons for marking it?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the sufficiency of the 'hady' (pilgrimage sacrifice) for the 'Udhiyah' (Eid sacrifice) highlights the flexibility in fulfilling sacrificial obligations within Shia jurisprudence. The mention of the 'illah' (legal cause) regarding marking and tagging the camel connects ritual purity with practical identification, ensuring the animal is distinct and ready for slaughter. This reflects the broader Shia emphasis on the intentionality and physical readiness of the sacrificial animal as key components of valid worship.
